did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title includes several details: it is attributed to the sons of Korah, attributed to Heman the Ezrahite, and also identified as a “maskil”—a psalm with a teaching or contemplative character.
Did you know? At the very beginning of the psalm, the poet addresses the LORD as “God of my salvation,” emphasizing that he cries out to Him both day and night.
Did you know? The poet describes his condition with images of nearness to death: his soul is filled with troubles, and his life has reached Sheol.
Did you know? In this verse, the poet compares himself to the dead and those slain in the grave, describing a sense of separation from the source of life and from active remembrance.
Did you know? The distress is depicted through images of depth and darkness: “the lowest pit,” “the dark places,” and “the depths.”
Did you know? The distress in the psalm is not merely internal: the poet says that his acquaintances have been kept far from him, and he feels confined and unable to get out.
Did you know? Although his eye is troubled by poverty and suffering, the poet continues to pray every day and stretch out his hands to the LORD.
Did you know? From this verse through verse 13, three consecutive questions appear about whether the dead can give thanks, acknowledge God’s steadfast love, and see the LORD’s wonders.
Did you know? The poet describes his prayer as one that comes before morning: “In the morning my prayer comes before You.”
Did you know? The psalm ends without an explicit description of resolution or salvation, and with the word “darkness”—emphasizing the sense of loneliness and darkness that continues to the very end.
